newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Bayernwerk plans to upgrade its Hungary utilities.
newsitem.headline: Bayernwerk plans to upgrade its Hungary utilities.

text.p: Germany's Bayernwerk AG plans further investments in Hungary's utilities in which it has stakes, company officials said.

"Our optimistic scenario is to invest 50 million marks per year in (electricity distributor) DEDASZ and some 60 million in (gas distributor) KOGAZ until the year 2000," Willi Gerner, a member of Bayernwerk's board, told a news conference on Wednesday, with the information embargoed until Thursday.
The company last December bought a 47.3 percent share in DEDASZ, and, jointly with Austria's EVN, a 50 percent plus one share stake in KOGAZ.
"We have invested some 500 million marks so far in Hungary," said Otto Majewski, president of Bayernwerk's board of directors, adding that an upgrade of the infrastructure was a must.
He said the company planned to bid again for core electricity company Magyar Villamos Muvek Rt (MVM) when it came on offer, probably at the beginning of next year.
"We are mainly interested in the high voltage grid," Majewski said.
Hungary's privatisation agency APV Rt declared a first tender unsuccessful in March, saying the bidders did not meet certain conditions.
Majewski said the tender would probably exclude Paks nuclear plant, which supplies almost half of Hungary's electricity.
He added that KOGAZ's 1996 results would be slightly in the red while DEDASZ would make some 10 million marks in losses this year.
This was partly the result of the government delaying until January 1 an energy price rise expected for October 1.
Majewski said Bayernwerk was in constant talks with the government about the planned price rise but declined to give any figures.
Bayernwerk did not intend to invest in building new power stations in Hungary, an official said.
"We see our role in future power stations as subcontractors rather than investors," said Rainer Frank Elsasser, a member of Bayernwerk's board.
The company, as owner of a regional gas supplier, is interested in the diversification of Hungary's gas imports, almost all of which come from Russia.
"The ideal proportion would be one third of imports coming from the West," Gerner said.
Bayernwerk regards its entry into Hungary's electricity market as a milestone and is committed to its presence in the country, Majewski said.
"Hungary could become a similar hub for electricity distribution as Switzerland is in the west."
